title: Homestay Social Media: What to Post and How Often
excerpt: A practical social media plan for family-run homestays: the host story, four things to post, a past-guest community, WhatsApp broadcasts and a sustainable rhythm.
description: Homestay social media made practical: tell the host story, post the place, food and neighbourhood, use WhatsApp broadcasts and keep a steady rhythm.
html:
Homestay social media works best when it shows what only a family-run stay has: the hosts, the home food, the place and the neighbourhood. Post a few times a week on Instagram, keep in touch with past guests through a WhatsApp broadcast list, and choose a rhythm the family can keep going in peak season.

What makes homestay social media different from a resort's

A resort sells facilities: a pool, a spa, a restaurant. A homestay sells a family and a way of living. Guests choose a homestay in Coorg, Wayanad, Spiti or the Northeast because they want to eat what the hosts eat, hear the stories of the estate or village, and feel looked after by people rather than staff. Your social media should show that, because it is the one thing a bigger property cannot copy.

This also means you do not need polished production. A clear phone video of your mother making akki rotti at breakfast says more than a drone shot.

Tell the host story first

Before you plan content, write down the story in a few lines. Guests and followers will come back to it again and again.

  • Who are the hosts, and how long has the family lived here?
  • Why did you start hosting guests?
  • What does a normal day look like on the property?
  • What do you love showing guests that they cannot find on their own?

Use this in your Instagram bio, a pinned post or highlight called "Our story", your Facebook page and your Google Business Profile description. Keep it in plain language. Mention the place name, because people search Instagram for places as much as for accounts.

What to post: four content buckets

Most homestays run out of ideas because they only post room photos. Spread your posts across four buckets instead.

BucketExamplesFormat that suits it
The placeMorning mist over the estate, the rooms after cleaning, the verandah at sunset, the monsoon gardenPhotos, short reels, carousels of each room
The foodBreakfast being cooked, a local dish and its story, fruit from the garden, a festival mealReels of cooking, close-up photos, recipe captions
The neighbourhoodA waterfall nearby, the weekly market, a temple festival, a trek route, how to reach in monsoonCarousels with travel tips, short videos, guides in highlights
The host familyHosts greeting guests, the dog, harvest season, grandmother's stories, the children helpingStories, informal reels, photos with longer captions

Always ask permission before posting guests, and never post children who are guests without their parents' clear consent. Family members who do not want to appear on camera should not have to.

Captions that do some work

A good caption tells a short story and answers a practical question. "Our kitchen garden gives us most of the vegetables for breakfast from June to September" is better than "Fresh food". Add the place name and one practical line, such as how long the drive from Mysuru takes, or what to pack for December.

Build a community with past guests

Your past guests are your best audience. They already trust you, they talk about their trip to friends, and many will come back.

  • At checkout, ask if they would like to follow your Instagram, and whether you can share any photos they send you.
  • Reshare guest stories when they tag you, with a thank-you message.
  • Reply to every comment and direct message, ideally the same day.
  • Post "then and now" or seasonal updates that remind past guests of their stay: "the jackfruit tree you sat under in April is now fruiting".
  • Invite past guests to suggest names for a new room or a new dish. Small requests keep people involved.

WhatsApp broadcast for repeat guests

Instagram reaches new people. WhatsApp keeps you close to people who have already stayed. A WhatsApp Business broadcast list sends one message to many contacts, each receiving it as a personal message. Broadcasts reach only people who have saved your number, so ask guests at checkout to save it.

Use broadcasts sparingly, perhaps once or twice a month, and make each one useful:

  • Availability for an upcoming long weekend.
  • A monsoon or weekday stay idea for returning guests.
  • A seasonal update: coffee blossom, orange harvest, first snowfall.
  • A new room or experience they might want to try.

Make it easy to opt out. If someone asks to stop, remove them straight away. Sending too often is the quickest way to get blocked or reported. Our guide to B&B direct bookings without a booking engine explains how to turn these replies into confirmed bookings.

A posting rhythm a family-run property can sustain

The best plan is the one that survives your busiest week. Many homestays post daily for a month, then stop for three months. A steady, smaller rhythm works better.

SeasonInstagram feed or reelsStoriesWhatsApp broadcast
Peak season (busy with guests)One or two a week, from content shot earlierA few a week, quick and casualRarely, only for cancellations or last-minute rooms
Shoulder seasonTwo or three a weekMost daysOnce or twice a month
Off-season or monsoonTwo or three a week, plus batch-shooting for the next peakMost daysOnce or twice a month with off-season offers

Practical habits

  • Pick one family member as the main owner of social media, with one helper.
  • Keep a shared phone album called "To post" and add five or ten photos every week.
  • Set aside one quiet morning a month to write captions and schedule posts with the platform's own scheduling tool.
  • Do not chase every trend. Pick one or two reel formats you are comfortable with and repeat them.

What to measure

Likes and followers are not bookings. Check a few simple things each month: how many enquiries came from Instagram or WhatsApp, how many became bookings, which posts led to direct messages, and how many past guests rebooked. Ask every new enquiry "how did you find us?" and note the answer in your booking sheet. For setting up proper tracking, see our analytics and reporting service.

Frequently asked questions

How often should a homestay post on Instagram?

Choose a rhythm you can keep through your busiest season, such as two or three posts a week plus stories most days, and drop to one or two posts a week in peak months. Regular posting over many months matters more than a burst of daily posts followed by silence. Shoot extra content in quiet periods so you have posts ready for busy weeks.

Should I post photos of my guests?

Only with clear permission, ideally asked before you take the photo. Many guests are happy to be featured and will reshare the post, but some want privacy. Never post guests' children without their parents' explicit consent. Resharing a story a guest has tagged you in is usually the simplest option, because they chose to share it.

Is WhatsApp broadcast better than Instagram for bookings?

They do different jobs. Instagram helps new people discover you and see what a stay is like. WhatsApp broadcast reaches past guests who already trust you, so their messages turn into bookings more directly. Most family-run homestays need both: Instagram for discovery and WhatsApp for repeat guests and quick enquiries. Keep broadcasts infrequent and useful.

Do I need to run ads on social media?

Not at the start. Build a consistent account with good photos, a clear story and some reviews first, because ads send people to your profile and they need something convincing to see. Once your organic posting is steady, small paid tests can extend your reach to travellers in your main source cities. Our separate guide covers Meta ads for homestays.

Where to start

Write your host story in five lines and put it in your Instagram bio and a pinned post. Create a shared "To post" album, plan two posts a week across the four buckets, and ask every departing guest to save your WhatsApp number. When you are ready to go beyond organic posting, read our guide to Meta ads for homestays.
